lead.t: Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) used to ensure adherence and prevent resistance (MDR-TB)

snip.t: Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) used to ensure adherence and prevent resistance (MDR-TB)

qs.q: Why is Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) strongly recommended when treating tuberculosis?
o: It ensures medication adherence and reduces acquired drug resistance
It shortens the total duration of active disease treatment to two months
It allows workers to administer all four drugs via a weekly injection
It eliminates the need to monitor patients for drug-induced hepatitis
qs.e: DOT involves a health care worker watching the patient swallow each dose, serving as the best way to ensure adherence and reduce relapse or acquired drug resistance.

faq.a: Because missed doses rapidly select resistant strains; observation ensures full course completion.
faq.q: Why is DOT preferred for MDR‑TB?

faq.a: Yes, if they are trained, reliable, and can document doses accurately.
faq.q: Can family members act as observers?

faq.a: Use community health workers, mobile DOT, or video‑observed therapy where feasible.
faq.q: What if a patient cannot attend the clinic daily?

exam: What are the three core components of DOT and why does each matter? — Observer presence, documentation, and patient education; they guarantee adherence, allow audit, and address barriers.

A patient with smear‑positive TB misses two consecutive DOT visits. What is your next step? — Contact the patient urgently, assess reasons, arrange alternative observer, and consider temporary inpatient isolation if infectious.
How does DOT reduce the emergence of MDR‑TB? — By preventing intermittent dosing that allows selective survival of resistant bacilli.

Compare DOT for TB with directly observed antiretroviral therapy (DOT‑ART). What are the similarities and key differences? — Both use observation, but DOT‑ART often uses community volunteers and has longer treatment duration; TB regimens are shorter but higher toxicity risk.

A rural clinic lacks GeneXpert. How would you decide to start DOT for a suspected TB case? — Use clinical criteria (cough >2 weeks, weight loss, chest X‑ray) and start empirical therapy with DOT, arranging referral for confirmatory testing when possible.
What red‑flag symptom during DOT warrants immediate referral to a higher‑level facility? — New haemoptysis, neurological deficits, or severe drug‑induced hepatitis.
Explain why ethambutol is avoided in a patient with known optic neuritis during DOT. — Ethambutol can worsen visual loss; alternative agents are chosen to prevent irreversible blindness.
How would you modify DOT for a pregnant woman with TB? — Use pregnancy‑safe first‑line drugs, ensure observer support, monitor liver function, and provide nutritional counseling.
ai.title: Directly Observed Therapy
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Directly observed therapy (DOT) is a strategy where a health worker watches patients take each dose of medication, improving adherence and preventing drug resistance, especially for TB in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: DOT is not a disease but a delivery model. It is applied when a prescribed regimen requires strict adherence, most commonly for tuberculosis (TB) and occasionally for HIV, hepatitis B, and malaria prophylaxis.

b: Mild disease may use self‑administered therapy
sections.p: The need for DOT is guided by disease severity: new smear‑positive pulmonary TB, multidrug‑resistant TB (MDR‑TB), and extrapulmonary TB with high bacterial load all mandate DOT.

b: HIV antiretroviral therapy in pilot programs
sections.p: Non‑adherence stems from poverty, stigma, side‑effects, and health‑system gaps. In East Africa, the most common indication for DOT is Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

Patients on DOT are usually identified during clinic visits for cough, weight loss, night sweats, or a positive sputum test. The clinician must assess readiness, social support, and potential barriers.
Tests confirm the underlying disease and monitor response; they are not for DOT itself.

t.b: Confirms TB and drug resistance; positive means active disease, resistance guides regimen
Assesses disease extent; cavitary disease predicts higher transmission risk
Detects co‑infection influencing regimen and need for integrated DOT

sections.p: Failure of DOT can lead to treatment default, relapse, and development of drug‑resistant TB, which carries high mortality.

b: First‑line TB: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol
sections.p: Implement DOT by assigning a reliable observer, documenting each dose, and providing patient education. Choose drug regimens per WHO guidelines; avoid drugs with high hepatotoxicity if liver disease is present.
Review patients weekly for the intensive phase, then monthly for continuation. Reinforce infection control, vaccinate contacts, and address socioeconomic barriers.
Self‑administered therapy (SAT) where patients take medicines without observation; both aim for adherence but DOT provides higher certainty.

b: Early conversion does not guarantee cure
sections.p: A negative sputum smear after two weeks may be falsely reassuring if specimen quality is poor; continue DOT until culture conversion.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe drug toxicity (e.g., visual loss from ethambutol)
